clue.text: Conceit natural in connection with stars

parts.note: side is an old word for swank or conceited airs, as in 'putting on side'
real means natural or genuine

explanation.surface: Someone describes vanity as something that comes naturally to celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' suggests celebrities and their vanity, but here they are heavenly bodies. SIDE is the dated British sense of pretentious airs.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidereal is the astronomer's adjective for anything measured against or relating to the fixed celestial bodies.

clue.text: Luke's birds, ten a penny, authorized price

definitions.text: Luke's birds, ten a penny, authorized price

parts.words: Luke's birds, ten a penny, authorized price
parts.note: in Luke's gospel in the Authorized Version, five small birds are sold for two farthings, which works out at ten for a penny

explanation.surface: A gospel bird is priced cheaply by official decree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Authorized' points to the Authorized (King James) Version: Luke 12:6 sells five for two farthings, and four farthings made an old British penny.
explanation.definitionFit: Luke 12:6 asks whether five sparrows are not sold for two farthings.

clue.text: Pluto shot wide and is fired

parts.note: Dis is the Roman god of the underworld, also called Pluto
a shot that goes wide has missed

explanation.surface: A footballer named Pluto fires wide and gets the sack.
explanation.walkthrough: Pluto is not the planet or the dog: it is the underworld god, whose other Roman name is DIS.
explanation.definitionFit: To be sacked from a job is to be let go, sent away by the employer.

clue.text: He turned writing into hard cash

definitions.text: He turned writing into hard cash

parts.words: He turned writing into hard cash
parts.note: reads as an author who made money, but refers to a Victorian novelist who wrote a novel titled Hard Cash

explanation.surface: An author successfully made money from his writing.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade's 1863 novel is called Hard Cash, so he literally turned writing into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Reade was the Victorian novelist who wrote Hard Cash and The Cloister and the Hearth.

clue.text: She gets a bit of money on the sound unit

parts.note: an anna was a small coin of British India, a sixteenth of a rupee
the bel is a unit of sound intensity, ten decibels

explanation.surface: A woman places a small coin on a hi-fi speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts ANNA above BEL in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Annabel is a woman's name, so it can stand for any female person.

clue.text: Abstemious operatic hero

parts.note: a temperate drinker might stop at a single glass of spirit, and Tchaikovsky's opera has a title role whose name splits that way

explanation.surface: A tenor in an opera is described as a teetotaller.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the name of Tchaikovsky's title character into two words and it describes a moderate drinker who has just a single measure of spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene Onegin is the title character of Tchaikovsky's opera, and the split form describes taking one drink only.

clue.text: Non-Orwell newspeak

parts.note: a newly coined word, new speech in general rather than the invented language of Nineteen Eighty-Four

explanation.surface: Fresh jargon that does not come from Orwell's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Newspeak is the language of Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four; without the capital it means simply new speech, a freshly coined term.
explanation.definitionFit: A neologism is a newly coined word or expression.

clue.text: Round-figure measurement

parts.note: not a rounded number but a measurement taken around the body or waist

explanation.surface: A measurement given as a convenient rounded number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round figure' suggests a rounded number; it is the measure round a figure, a waistline.
explanation.definitionFit: Girth is the distance round something, such as a waist.

clue.text: Rung up about lack of trade

definitions.text: Rung up about lack of trade

parts.words: Rung up about lack of trade
parts.note: a till entry made to open the drawer when nothing is sold

explanation.surface: Someone phones to complain that business is slack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rung up' sounds like a phone call; it is a shop till being rung when no purchase is made.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-sale entry on a cash register opens the drawer without recording any purchase.

clue.text: He gets a free seat for the review

definitions.text: He gets a free seat for the review

parts.words: He gets a free seat for the review
parts.note: a reviewer given complimentary tickets so he can write about a show

explanation.surface: A man is given a free ticket for a theatre revue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Review' sounds like a revue, a show; it is the write-up he is given the seat to produce.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre reviewer is given press seats in return for writing about the show.

clue.text: He's quite dry, though rain beats wildly

indicators.note: beats wildly tells us the letters of rain and beats are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone stays dry even though rain is pounding down in a storm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dry' looks like weather, but it means teetotal. The anagram signal 'wildly' rearranges RAIN plus BEATS.
explanation.definitionFit: A teetotaller is called dry because no alcohol passes his lips.

clue.text: Fragrant root of a Latin poet, we 'ear ?

indicators.note: the dropped h of 'ear mimics a Cockney speaker, so the poet's name is said with its first letter dropped

parts.note: Horace was a Roman lyric poet

explanation.surface: A scented root is said to belong to a Roman poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The Cockney 'ear tells you to drop the H: Horace said that way, ''Orace', sounds like ORRIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Orris is the dried rootstock of an iris, used in perfumery for its violet scent.

clue.text: It flows with water as its land with wine

definitions.text: It flows with water as its land with wine

parts.words: It flows with water as its land with wine
parts.note: a German river whose valley is famous vineyard country, so its water flows as its vineyards flow with hock

explanation.surface: A land that flows with wine as a river does with water.
explanation.definitionFit: The great German river runs between some of Europe's most famous vineyards, source of hock.

clue.text: Engagement at stake ? Rubbish, Henry

parts.note: money at stake is a wager or bet
rot means nonsense or rubbish
Hal is a familiar form of Henry, as with Shakespeare's Prince Hal

explanation.surface: An engagement with something on the line is dismissed as rubbish by a man named Henry.
explanation.definitionFit: A betrothal is a formal promise to marry, the same thing as being engaged.

clue.text: Profligate lets war loose

indicators.note: let loose tells us the letters of lets and war are set free into a new order

explanation.surface: A reckless ruler unleashes a war.
explanation.definitionFit: A wastrel is a spendthrift good-for-nothing, the same as a profligate person.

clue.text: Voting qualification: commonly desirable for an agent

definitions.text: Voting qualification: commonly desirable for an agent

parts.words: Voting qualification: commonly desirable for an agent
parts.note: living in a constituency qualifies one to vote, and estate agents habitually call a home 'desirable'

explanation.surface: An official explains what makes a voter eligible and what agents like.
explanation.walkthrough: British estate agents' cliché is 'a desirable residence'; a place of abode is also a voting qualification.
explanation.definitionFit: Living in a district gives the right to vote there, and an agent advertises a home as a desirable one.

clue.text: They mark musical time by going on strike

definitions.text: They mark musical time by going on strike

parts.words: They mark musical time by going on strike
parts.note: reads like workers walking out, but it is bells sounding the hours as a clock strikes

explanation.surface: Musicians stop work in an industrial dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strike' suggests a walkout; clock bells strike the hour and mark time tunefully.
explanation.definitionFit: Chimes are tuned bells that ring out the hours when a clock strikes.

clue.text: Don't blame the old single-speed !

parts.note: ex is a prefix meaning former, hence old
one means single
rate means speed, as in the rate of travel

explanation.surface: A plea not to criticise an old bicycle with only one gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Single-speed' suggests a bicycle with one gear, but it splits into two pieces; 'Don't blame' is the definition read as an order.
explanation.definitionFit: To exonerate someone is to clear them of blame, as an imperative telling us not to accuse.

clue.text: Alienate and set wandering over the mountains

indicators.note: in a down clue, over places the first piece on top of the second
wandering tells us the letters of set roam into a new order

parts.note: a range is a chain of mountains

explanation.surface: Someone drifts apart and sets off roaming across the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set wandering' gives EST, an anagram of SET, sitting over RANGE in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To estrange people is to make them hostile or distant, to turn them away from each other.

clue.text: Inventor of 20 perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the answer to clue 20 is only one possible arrangement of these letters

parts.note: the answer to 20 down, a word meaning spread about as rumour

explanation.surface: A clue asks who might have devised the item numbered twenty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of 20' looks like the thing he invented, but 'perhaps' rearranges the letters of the answer to 20 down.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Edison was the American who devised the phonograph and a practical electric light bulb.

clue.text: How a rumour is treated abroad

definitions.text: How a rumour is treated abroad

parts.words: How a rumour is treated abroad
parts.note: the old phrase for spreading gossip widely is that it is talked about everywhere

explanation.surface: A question about how foreigners handle gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' suggests foreign countries, but it means widely about, as in the biblical phrase for a rumour spread about.
explanation.definitionFit: To noise something abroad is to spread it widely as a report.

clue.text: Public grounds of Government House

definitions.meaning: common land shared by the people of a parish or town
the lower chamber of the British Parliament is the House of the same name

explanation.surface: Open land belongs to the official residence of a governor.
explanation.definitionFit: Shared parkland is common land, and the elected lower chamber at Westminster is the House of this name.

clue.text: City from the field of letters

indicators.note: taking from tells us the word field is removed

parts.note: Lord Chesterfield is famous for his letters of advice to his son
the word field as written

explanation.surface: A town is said to come from the world of literature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Field of letters' suggests literature; it is Lord Chesterfield of the Letters, with FIELD taken away to leave the city.
explanation.definitionFit: Chester is a cathedral city in Cheshire, England.

clue.text: Aim of state opposition

explanation.surface: The purpose of opposition in a nation's politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a nation; it is the verb, to say.
explanation.definitionFit: A purpose is one's goal, and to protest is to raise an objection.

clue.text: Main artillery attack along minor highway

parts.note: a B-road is a British secondary road, below an A-road
alongside, or at the side of, something

explanation.surface: Guns open fire on traffic along a country road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' is the sea, so the definition is a naval attack. Britain grades roads A and B, a B road being the lesser kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadside is the simultaneous firing of all guns on one side of a warship on the open sea.

clue.text: Deck or trim branches

parts.note: to lop a tree is to cut off its branches

explanation.surface: A choice between decorating or pruning a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deck' looks like a verb, to adorn; it is a ship's deck.
explanation.definitionFit: The orlop is the lowest deck of a sailing ship.

clue.text: Ox and cox

definitions.meaning: a castrated bullock raised for beef
to cox a boat is to direct its course

explanation.surface: A bullock and a rowing coxswain are set side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A young castrated bull reared for beef is a bullock of this name, and a coxswain's job is to guide the boat.

clue.text: Irrational quantities

parts.note: mathematical roots that cannot be written as a fraction

explanation.surface: Amounts that make no sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A surd is a root such as the square root of two, which no fraction can express exactly.

clue.text: Nellie is back, but I'm wanting another

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the letter that I'm points to is removed
is back means the name Nellie is read from right to left

parts.note: the speaker's self, the letter I

explanation.surface: Nellie has returned, yet the speaker longs for a different girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is back' turns NELLIE to EILLEN; 'wanting' then drops the I to leave ELLEN, another girl's name like Nellie.
explanation.definitionFit: Ellen is a girl's name, a different woman from the Nellie of the clue.

clue.text: Join Territorials in harbour

parts.note: to enter a club or the army is to join it
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: Volunteer soldiers sign up at a port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harbour' looks like a port; here it is the verb, as in harbouring a thought.
explanation.definitionFit: To harbour a hope or doubt is to hold it in mind, to entertain it.

clue.text: Rise above the confusion. It's hell !

parts.note: to top something is to rise above it

indicators.note: the confusion means the letters of the word the are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone urged to rise above chaos complains that it is hell.
explanation.definitionFit: Tophet is a biblical place near Jerusalem used in literature as a name for the infernal pit.

clue.text: Rare gems from poetic lake-village

indicators.note: from signals that the answer is made out of the reordered letters of rare and gems

explanation.surface: Precious stones are found in a Lake District village loved by poets.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lake District village on its own lake was Wordsworth's home, hence 'poetic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Grasmere is the Cumbrian village and lake where Wordsworth lived at Dove Cottage.
